title: Scam Offensives in Southeast Asia: Comparing Beijing's and Washington's Strategies and Assessing Opportunities for Coordination
gist: A long ASPI report arguing that Asia's $88–114 billion cyber scam industry is one of the few genuine U.S.-China common interests, that Beijing's crackdowns are selective and triggered only by domestic anger, BRI reputational damage, or border proximity, and that Washington's sanctions-and-indictment playbook works mainly as a trigger that raises the political cost for Beijing and host states — as with the Chen Zhi/Prince Group case and the $15 billion seizure.

themes.theme: Scale and economics of the scam industry

insights.claim: Asia's cyber scam industry is valued at between $88.3 billion and $114.1 billion annually, run predominantly out of Myanmar, Cambodia, and Laos and targeting both Chinese and American citizens.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Sizes an illicit sector larger than many national economies — the enforcement, compliance and crypto-tracing spend attached to it scales with this number.
insights.quote: which is valued at between $88.3 billion and $114.1 billion annually
insights.locator: Executive Summary — Disrupting Asia’s cyber scam industry

insights.claim: Americans lost $17.6 billion to cyber-enabled fraud in 2025, with most of that money flowing to Chinese-linked transnational crime groups operating out of Myanmar, Laos, and Cambodia.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: A hard baseline for U.S. consumer fraud loss growth — relevant to bank/fintech fraud reserves, payments-risk vendors and crypto compliance demand.
insights.quote: In 2025, Americans lost $17.6 billion to cyber-enabled fraud
insights.locator: State of the Scam Industry

insights.claim: Chinese national losses to cyber fraud rose from $5.5 billion in 2021 to an estimated $33.8 billion by 2023, which is what forced Beijing into joint operations with Myanmar's junta.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Quantifies the domestic-loss threshold at which Beijing converts a foreign-policy irritant into a cross-border enforcement campaign.

insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Explains why Cambodian crackdowns stay cosmetic: genuine eradication would be a macro shock to the country, so pledges should be discounted heavily.

insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Enforcement in one jurisdiction is a targeting-reallocation event, not a supply reduction — the single most tradeable insight in the paper for fraud-exposed firms.

insights.claim: Recent field research cited in the paper suggests that between 30,000 and 35,000 scammers may still have been working within the Golden Triangle Special Economic Zone in Laos as of May 2026.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Laos is the untouched reservoir — a leading indicator of where displaced Cambodian capacity lands next.
insights.quote: between 30,000 and 35,000 scammers may still be working within the Golden Triangle Economic Zone
insights.locator: Recent field research by Jason Tower

insights.claim: Amnesty International found that more than 70% of the Cambodian scam compounds it tracked were essentially bypassed by the 2026 crackdown and remain operational, despite official claims of 488 locations raided and nearly 16,000 people deported.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Treat Cambodian enforcement statistics as political output, not compliance progress — the gap is the tell for anyone pricing Cambodia tariff or sanctions risk.
insights.quote: more than 70% of the scam compounds they tracked were essentially bypassed and remain operational

themes.theme: Three-factor model of when Beijing acts

insights.claim: China's anti-scam enforcement abroad is driven by three factors — expression of domestic discontent, reputational damage to China's image and the Belt and Road Initiative, and geographic proximity to Chinese territory — and its intensity tracks how many of the three converge.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: A predictive screen: score any Chinese-linked illicit hub on these three variables to forecast whether Beijing intervenes, stalls, or protects.
insights.quote: the expression of domestic discontent, reputational damage to China’s image and its Belt and Road Initiative, and the geographic proximity of scam operations to Chinese territory
insights.locator: When China Acts—And When It Does Not

insights.claim: In Myanmar, where all three drivers converge, Beijing acted forcefully: more than 41,000 scam suspects were handed over during Operation 1027 and Chinese authorities and the junta announced more than 57,000 Chinese nationals arrested since 2023.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Shows the ceiling of Chinese enforcement capacity when political will exists — and that the constraint elsewhere is will, not capability.
insights.quote: more than 41,000 scam suspects had been handed over from authorities in northern Myanmar as part of Operation 1027
insights.locator: Frustrated with what they viewed as insufficient cooperation

insights.claim: Beijing had opened a police investigation into Chen Zhi in 2020 but only publicly called for his arrest and extradition after the 2025 U.S. indictment and joint U.S.-UK sanctions, leading experts to conclude the U.S. action was the trigger.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: The operative U.S. lever on protected Chinese-linked actors is reputational: a high-profile indictment can force a Beijing arrest years ahead of its own timetable.
insights.quote: This has led experts to suggest that it was the indictment and sanctions that finally triggered Beijing to act.
insights.locator: In Cambodia, the primary catalyst for Chinese action

insights.claim: Laos shows what happens when none of the three drivers applies: the Golden Triangle SEZ lacks border proximity, gets less coverage, and its operator Zhao Wei — decorated by the Lao government, a CCP supporter with party-state ties from the 1990s — has faced no enforcement action on the scale of the Chen Zhi indictment.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Zhao Wei is the test case: a high-profile U.S. designation of him would be the cheapest way to test whether the Chen Zhi trigger mechanism generalizes.
insights.locator: Laos is an example of what happens when none

insights.claim: Beijing has historically been agnostic toward how CCP-supporting actors pursue claimed national interests abroad, until those actors are perceived as harming Chinese citizens and China's reputation.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Reputational harm — not legality — is the trip-wire; campaigns that generate Chinese-language outrage are more effective than legal argument.
insights.quote: Beijing has historically been agnostic toward how actors that support the CCP pursue what they claim are national interests abroad, until they are perceived by Beijing as harming Chinese citizens and China’s reputation.
insights.locator: Taken together, the divergent fates of Chen Zhi

insights.claim: The U.S. Select Committee on China concluded in May 2026 that there is no top-down command of the scam industry from Beijing, but that PRC-origin criminal networks and CCP-linked actors repeatedly benefited from selective enforcement, political protection, illicit finance and opaque infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Undercuts the maximalist 'state-directed' narrative — useful for calibrating how far U.S. escalation against China itself, versus against individual actors, is justified.
insights.quote: PRC-origin criminal networks and CCP-linked actors have repeatedly benefited from systems of selective enforcement, political protection, illicit finance, and opaque infrastructure.
insights.locator: In May 2026, the U.S. Select Committee on China

insights.claim: Viral domestic incidents function as the forcing mechanism for Chinese enforcement: after actor Wang Xing's 2025 abduction from Mae Sot went viral, more than 1,800 Chinese nationals posted demands for rescue and MPS announced it would 'relentlessly pursue and crack down' on overseas gangs, leading to 5,400 repatriations from Myawaddy by July.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Chinese social media virality is a real-time leading indicator of imminent cross-border police operations in the Mekong.
insights.quote: relentlessly pursue and crack down
insights.locator: Another wave of Chinese action in Myanmar followed

themes.theme: GSI and China's expanding security footprint

insights.claim: Anti-scam enforcement marks a pivot away from China's long-standing noninterference doctrine, with Beijing explicitly linking overseas police operations to the Global Security Initiative launched in April 2022.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Transnational crime is the acceptable wrapper for Chinese extraterritorial policing — expect the same template in Africa and the Gulf next.
insights.quote: have marked a pivot away from Beijing’s long-standing policy of noninterference in the affairs of other countries
insights.locator: Beijing's Global Security Initiative Expands in the Mekong

insights.claim: The Lancang-Mekong Integrated Law Enforcement and Security Cooperation Center in Kunming has been the principal channel since 2023 for joint operations across China, Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar, Thailand and Vietnam, with its 2024 Operation SEAGULL reportedly cracking 160+ cases and arresting more than 70,000 suspects.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: The institutional plumbing already exists for China-led regional policing; any U.S. cooperation would be plugging into Chinese-built architecture.
insights.quote: more than 160 cases cracked, more than 70,000 criminal suspects arrested
insights.locator: The Lancang-Mekong Integrated Law Enforcement

insights.claim: Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar and Thailand accounted for 26 of the 192 bilateral security meetings held by China's Ministry of Public Security between mid-2022 and mid-2025, showing Beijing has used the scam epidemic to deepen security ties rather than only to solve a crime problem.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Quantifies the diplomatic return Beijing is earning from the crackdown — the security-relationship payoff is the reason enforcement persists.
insights.quote: 26 of the 192 bilateral security meetings held by MPS between mid-2022 and mid-2025
insights.locator: Conversely, China has leveraged the scam epidemic

insights.claim: China's leverage map is institutional: it holds a 1999 extradition treaty and a permanent police presence in Cambodia since 2019, an extradition treaty with Laos since 2002 plus police stations along the Mekong, but no extradition treaty or permanent police presence in Myanmar.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Predicts which country can deliver an extradition on demand — Cambodia can, Myanmar cannot, which is why Myanmar enforcement takes the form of mass repatriation instead.
insights.locator: Although there have been fewer joint China-Cambodia

insights.claim: Thailand has been the most resistant Mekong partner to Chinese policing, with backlash over Assistant Minister Liu Zhongyi moving freely across the Thai border in February 2025 forcing him to apologize to Thailand's defense minister for perceived infringement on Thai sovereignty.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Sovereignty friction caps how far Chinese security expansion can run in treaty-partner states — the opening Washington can work through Bangkok.
insights.quote: a remarkable concession that nonetheless underscored how far operational realities had drifted from normal diplomatic protocol
insights.locator: Tensions came to a head in February 2025

insights.claim: China's anti-scam campaign has doubled as surveillance export: Huawei has installed a city-wide surveillance grid in Bangkok and Chinese companies built the Lao Ministry of Public Security's police internet infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Every escalation of the scam crisis is a demand catalyst for Chinese public-security tech vendors across ASEAN.
insights.quote: In Bangkok, Huawei has installed a city-wide surveillance grid.
insights.locator: Beyond amplifying intelligence-sharing and operational agreements

insights.claim: The U.S. approach relies on sanctions, indictments and asset seizures rather than on-the-ground operations, because any arrest in Southeast Asia is conditional on local cooperation while Beijing holds both the ability and leverage to detain key actors.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: U.S. tools move money and reputations, not bodies — so measure U.S. impact by whether Beijing or a host state subsequently arrests someone.
insights.locator: Washington's Strategy for Addressing Southeast Asia's Scam Economy

insights.claim: The October 2025 Chen Zhi action combined a DOJ indictment, the seizure of $15 billion in assets — described as the largest criminal asset seizure in history — and coordinated U.S.-UK sanctions on 146 targets tied to the Prince Group.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Sets the template and scale for future designations; also creates a $15 billion pool of contested crypto assets whose ownership is unresolved.
insights.quote: seized nearly $15 billion in assets connected to his operations—the largest criminal asset seizure in history
insights.locator: In October 2025, the U.S. Department of Justice

insights.claim: U.S. trade negotiators gave Cambodia a 90-day window to show progress dismantling scam centers as a condition for tariff relief, explicitly linking cyber scam enforcement to economic statecraft.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Scam-center compliance is now a live variable in Cambodian tariff and market-access outcomes — a directly tradeable policy linkage.
insights.quote: gave Cambodia a 90-day window to demonstrate progress on dismantling scam centers as a condition for tariff relief
insights.locator: Although not part of the same announcement

insights.claim: The Scam Center Strike Force created in November 2025 has four mandates: seize and disable U.S.-based scam-enabling infrastructure, charge compound leaders, trace and seize stolen cryptocurrency, and prevent victimization through public education.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Crypto tracing and infrastructure takedown are institutionalized U.S. workstreams now — sustained demand for blockchain analytics and exchange compliance.
insights.locator: Efforts to combat cybercrime across several arms

insights.claim: U.S. intelligence access depends on Thailand: American law enforcement embedded in the Royal Thai Police War Room obtained 8,000 phones and 1,500 computers from the KNLA's November raid on the Shunda compound, enabling wire fraud conspiracy charges against Huang Xing Shan and Jiang Wei.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Thailand is the single point of failure in the U.S. evidence chain; the indictment also legitimizes ethnic armed organizations as intelligence partners.
insights.quote: 8,000 phones and 1,500 computers were handed over to Thai law enforcement
insights.locator: One substantial trove of intelligence

insights.claim: Defunding Radio Free Asia and the U.S. Institute of Peace cut the evidence pipeline that produced U.S. enforcement actions, since RFA reporting was critical to scrutiny of Chen Zhi and USIP's 2024 study first sized the industry for Washington.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: A self-inflicted degradation of the intelligence base for sanctions — expect fewer well-evidenced designations over time unless civil society funding is restored.
insights.quote: Reporting from Radio Free Asia, which has been defunded by the Trump administration, was critical to building international scrutiny of Chen Zhi and the Prince Group’s activities.
insights.locator: Above all, to both support the intelligence gathering

themes.theme: Intelligence asymmetry and the trust deficit

insights.claim: Seized devices are the sharpest friction point because they contain victims' financial and identity data alongside evidence of protection arrangements — a counterintelligence risk for Washington and a state-linkage exposure risk for Beijing.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Any cooperation deal will stall on device custody first; watch for third-party custody arrangements as the tell that talks are real.
insights.quote: Devices seized in these operations are intelligence troves
insights.locator: Intelligence is a sharp point of friction

insights.claim: Chen Zhi's extradition to China was likely timed in close succession to U.S. charges specifically to ensure he never reached an American courtroom, and Beijing is unlikely to cede any high-level Chinese national to the United States where extradition requests compete.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: U.S. indictments of Chinese-linked principals should be expected to yield Chinese custody, not U.S. custody — plan enforcement value around disruption, not prosecution.
insights.quote: Chen Zhi’s extradition to China was likely initiated in such close succession to the announcement of U.S. charges to ensure that Chen never made it to an American courtroom
insights.locator: High-level operators themselves are troves of intelligence

insights.claim: Working with Beijing on joint raids carries the risk of involuntary repatriation and prosecution of trafficked workers, since China has published only a few isolated cases classifying repatriated scammers as trafficking victims.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: A hard legal and reputational constraint on U.S. participation — any joint-raid framework needs a victim-screening carve-out to survive scrutiny.
insights.locator: The United States and China likewise diverge

insights.claim: The two sides hold complementary and non-substitutable intelligence: the United States cannot map the syndicates' China-facing infrastructure, and China cannot see the dollar-denominated financial flows that U.S. investigators are best positioned to trace.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: This asymmetry is the actual basis for any deal — and explains why the $15 billion seizure is hard to attribute without PRC shadow-banking data.
insights.quote: the United States cannot map the syndicates’ China-facing infrastructure, and China cannot see the dollar-denominated financial flows that U.S. investigators are best positioned to trace
insights.locator: Both the United States and China have intelligence

insights.claim: The U.S. Attorney's Office is having serious challenges determining who the $15 billion confiscated in the Chen Zhi case belongs to, because scam laundering is routed through PRC-based shadow banking systems.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Victim restitution from the largest seizure in history is far from automatic; the legal overhang on those assets is multi-year.
insights.locator: While the United States has had success in seizing stolen funds

insights.claim: The deepest misalignment is that each country protects its own citizens first, so nationally siloed enforcement guarantees syndicates simply rotate toward whichever victim population is least defended — and will swing back to Mandarin speakers when Beijing eases off.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Expect a reversion in targeting when Chinese operational tempo drops — a forecastable rotation in where fraud losses land.
insights.quote: as soon as Chinese officials take their foot off the pedal, crime syndicates will shift back to targeting the Mandarin-speaking world
insights.locator: However, it is this whack-a-mole nature

themes.theme: Host-state political economy as the binding constraint

insights.claim: Scam operations in Myanmar, Cambodia and Laos are not merely tolerated by weak states but embedded in the revenue streams and patronage networks of governing elites, so host governments are incentivized to manage external pressure rather than eliminate its source.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Treat host-state political economy, not enforcement capacity, as the binding constraint when forecasting whether any crackdown sticks.
insights.quote: scam operations are not simply tolerated by weak states but are embedded in the revenue streams and patronage networks of governing elites
insights.locator: Any account of U.S.-China misalignment

insights.claim: Host states convert great-power competition into regime protection: under U.S. pressure Myanmar's junta arrested 2,198 low-level KK Park operators while shielding affiliated militia leaders, then framed U.S. concern as a hidden agenda it knew would alarm Beijing.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Arrest counts are a deflection metric; the signal is whether militia leaders or protected owners are ever touched.
insights.quote: hidden agenda
insights.locator: For example, when Washington escalated pressure

insights.claim: Cambodian raids have been systematically pre-leaked: owners tipped off ahead of 2022 police raids bussed workers into the countryside, the majority of raided compounds reopened two months later, and no charges were filed against syndicates or owners.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: The two-month reopening cycle is the base rate against which to judge any new Cambodian or Lao enforcement announcement.
insights.quote: The majority of raided compounds reopened just two months later, and no charges were filed against syndicates or owners.
insights.locator: By 2022, China raised pressure on the Cambodian government

insights.claim: Chinese nationals such as Chen Zhi bought Cambodian citizenship to reduce extradition risk and deepen integration into local protection networks, while Chen served as an advisor to both Hun Sen and Hun Manet.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Citizenship-by-investment programs in host states are an operational sanctions-evasion tool, and a screening flag for compliance teams.
insights.quote: Many Chinese nationals such as Chen paid for Cambodian citizenship to reduce extradition risk
insights.locator: Only operations run by politically connected elites

insights.claim: The fentanyl negotiations are the working template: Washington raised the reputational cost of Beijing's inaction with indictments, sanctions and publicity, then paid for movement with a fentanyl tariff reduction, port fee suspension and trade truce extension — implying similar U.S. concessions will be needed on scams.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Anti-scam cooperation is likely to be paid for in trade concessions — watch for scam language appearing alongside tariff or port-fee items in any Trump-Xi deliverable.
insights.locator: The U.S. campaign to force fentanyl onto the bilateral agenda

insights.claim: The April 2026 Dubai joint raid — the United States, China, Thailand and the UAE arresting 276 telecom fraud suspects — was deliberately timed two weeks before a Trump-Xi meeting in Beijing as a mutual goodwill signal, and a similar operation before September's summit is being urged.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Joint anti-scam raids are a leading indicator of U.S.-China summit atmospherics — watch for one ahead of the September visit, APEC or the G20.
insights.quote: The timing of the Dubai joint raid in April, just two weeks before Trump and Xi met in Beijing, was not incidental
insights.locator: While Chen Zhi’s sanctions and arrest unfolded

insights.claim: Beijing published no repatriation numbers after the Dubai raid, which — given how routinely it publicizes crackdown metrics — suggests the 276 arrested were mostly not Chinese nationals, and implies custody transfers get easier as compounds staff up with non-Chinese workers.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: A clever read-through: absence of Chinese publicity is a diagnostic for the nationality mix of a raid, and for how much reputational skin Beijing has in the operation.
insights.quote: Beijing has not published any repatriation numbers
insights.locator: The Dubai raid is likely an example of this demographic shift

insights.claim: Thailand's SHIELD platform, launched in early July as the first system purpose-built to integrate scam and trafficking intelligence, has already been adopted by partners in ten countries including both China and the United States.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: SHIELD is the most concrete existing venue where U.S. and Chinese anti-scam data could actually meet — a low-visibility indicator worth tracking.
insights.quote: Thai police report that SHIELD has already been adopted by partners in ten countries, including China and the United States
insights.locator: In early July, Thailand launched SHIELD

insights.claim: The United States should approach Beijing with intelligence it lacks, sourcing it from Philippine POGO device troves seized from 2012–2019 gaming operations, and from the roughly 200,000 workers from 35 countries Cambodian officials say were released in the 2026 crackdown.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Identifies two concrete, underexploited intelligence reservoirs that would change the U.S. bargaining position with MPS.
insights.quote: Cambodian officials report that some 200,000 workers from 35 countries have been released
insights.locator: A vast amount of intelligence can be gathered

insights.claim: The U.S. private sector holds the leverage Beijing lacks: Tether has repeatedly cooperated with DOJ and OFAC to freeze pig-butchering assets, Meta's platforms are the primary channel between syndicates and Western victims, and Starlink terminal geolocation offers a near-real-time map of compound activity for which DOJ has already issued seizure warrants.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Concrete, name-level exposure: stablecoin issuers, social platforms and satellite connectivity providers are now instruments of U.S. anti-scam statecraft — and carry the attendant regulatory and privacy risk.
insights.quote: Starlink’s terminal geolocation data offers a near-real-time map of compound activity in ungoverned areas of Myanmar, for which the DOJ has already issued seizure warrants
insights.locator: Several other private sector companies based in the United States

insights.claim: The 2015 FinCEN–CAMLMAC memorandum of understanding created a U.S.-China financial intelligence channel that has never produced a publicly reported exchange, case or joint product, and reactivating it would fill the operational gap that high-level dialogues cannot.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: A dormant, below-the-political-line channel is the cheapest available cooperation upgrade — its activation would be a real signal, unlike ministerial communiqués.
insights.quote: neither FinCEN nor the Treasury Department has publicly reported any exchanges, cases, or joint products under the MOU since its signing
insights.locator: Leverage Existing Channels for Financial Intelligence Sharing

insights.claim: Sharing joint target lists is politically unrealistic because sanctions packages are guarded to stop targets from moving money, so Washington's usable lever is sequencing its own high-profile indictments against names already on China's MPS wanted notices.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: MPS wanted notices are a public, free signal of where U.S. and Chinese enforcement interests overlap — the highest-probability targets for actual arrests.
insights.locator: Incentivize China to Continue Extraditing Key Actors

insights.claim: Because China withholds the names of politically sensitive targets, public signals are an incomplete guide to alignment and the United States should expect competing extradition requests whenever it pursues an unnamed actor — with the Tokyo arrest of a Chinese-born Cypriot Prince Group executive shaping up as the test case.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: A near-term, observable test of whether U.S. partners extradite to Washington or Beijing when both ask — watch the Tokyo case.
insights.quote: if they both do, this will serve as a test case of who the U.S.-partners choose to extradite to
insights.locator: Endnotes — As of writing in August 2026, Tokyo has under arrest

insights.claim: China's operational surge against scams is not sustainable indefinitely, and the industry is evolving with AI and expanding into regions where Beijing has little security presence — which is the core argument that cooperation is time-limited.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: There is a closing window for a U.S.-China deal; after it, enforcement reverts to national silos and global fraud losses re-accelerate.
insights.quote: it cannot afford to give it this amount of attention forever, especially as the industry evolves with AI and expands to regions where China has less of an established security presence
